summary: Barrett Rock Light at the entrance to Prince Rupert harbour: a concrete tower and fog alarm built 1919-20 on a reef; reached only by boat, the tower now closed to visitors.

structures.note: Combined concrete light tower and fog alarm built in the year to 31 March 1920 (Department report); LighthouseFriends gives 1919 and says it was 40 feet tall. LighthouseFriends says it cracked after being struck by a fishing vessel (undated). Whether this concrete tower still stands is not stated in the sources read.

Present tower: white square tower with a red band (CCG list, 4.6 m). LighthouseFriends describes a white square skeletal tower with a red band in 2020; Rowlett describes a round white tower, 7 m, atop a square stone tower. The descriptions disagree; the CCG list is used here.
Combined keeper's dwelling and engine room of wood on the shore opposite the rock (Department report, year to 31 March 1920); LighthouseFriends places it on Barrett Point.

staffing.note: LighthouseFriends says the station was supposedly de-staffed in 1963, but Light Lists show resident personnel through 1973.

access.note: Reached only by boat. Owned and managed by the Canadian Coast Guard. Site open, tower closed (Rowlett).

visit.note: The tower is closed to visitors. LighthouseFriends says the light is easily seen from the ferry that calls at Prince Rupert.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends says E. H. Shockley built the tower in 1919. The Department's report places the construction in the year to 31 March 1920, so the build year is given as 1919 with the report's year noted.

The sources describe three different present-day towers: a 4.6 m white square tower with a red band (CCG), a white square skeletal tower with a red band (LighthouseFriends, 2020), and a round white 7 m tower atop a square stone tower (Rowlett). No source read says whether the 1919-20 concrete tower still stands.

notes_for_editor: Moderate evidence, mostly LighthouseFriends. The Department's 1920 report (year to 31 March 1920) gives the construction. The 1907-08 buoy list (1908 volume, p. 60; the 1909 volume p. 16 lists the same buoy) gives a Barrett Ledge in Chatham Sound that may be a different feature; the story says so. Everything else about keepers, the 1936 stranding, the undated Nemesis collision and the 1963/1973 staffing rests on LighthouseFriends alone. The Department's 1920s reports in the local corpus (which ends in 1924) name no keepers for this station. LighthouseFriends' own 1919 notice (unwatched light) and its keeper James Hall (first keeper of the light and fog alarm) are not reconciled; the story states both. The 1923 works list in the Marine report printed in 1924 (corpus label 1923, scan 37, printed 30) records a fog alarm building built under contract by E. H. Shockley and an installation of engines, compressors and diaphone on a line whose station heading the OCR does not show; it may refer to this station or to another (Lawyer Island is on the same list). It is not used. Name collisions: 'Barrett Ledge' also appears in the Quebec buoy lists (Father Point and Rimouski), and a 'Barret rock' is in Nova Scotia's Minas Basin list; neither is this station. 'Barrett rock' in the 1920 report is this station. The 1963 de-staffing statement is LighthouseFriends' own ('supposedly'); Light Lists were not checked. Record check: the coordinates match the CCG list; the record's first_lit is null. The 1920 value comes from the 1919 notice (light planned for about 1 March 1920); the Department report (year to 31 March 1920) does not confirm the lighting date. The record's structure note (tower standing, 4.6 m) matches the CCG list. The Prince Rupert City and Regional Archives was not searched. The 1936 Newington stranding is not in the corpus (which ends in 1924). Shape: six chapter headings for a moderate-length story (586 words); the two-to-four chapter guidance is not followed, and the chapters can be merged if the editor prefers.
